newsitem.title: INDIA: Sharif tells Bhutto to concede in Pakistan polls.
newsitem.headline: Sharif tells Bhutto to concede in Pakistan polls.

text.p: Nawaz Sharif, the clear winner of Pakistan's elections, on Tuesday urged his opponent Benazir Bhutto to accept defeat gracefully.
"I see no reason why she should not accept these results," the Pakistan Muslim League (PML) leader told Reuters as he headed for a stunning victory in national and provincial polls.
Jubilant PML supporters thronged Sharif's sprawling residence in Lahore, dancing, beating drums and singing.
With results declared for 166 of the National Assembly's 217 seats, the PML had won 117 seats, giving it a clear majority. Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) had won only 12.

"She (Bhutto) must accept the verdict of the people of Pakistan," Sharif said. "These were free and fair elections under the observation of foreign observers and the army, which deployed 250,000 men to ensure that there was no rigging.
"These elections were absolutely fair. She's a bad loser and she must accept this defeat."
PPP sources had said on Tuesday that Bhutto may boycott the national and provincial assemblies.
The PML's electoral ally, the Awami National Party, had won eight seats representing North West Frontier Province.

The Karachi-based ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM), which boycotted the last National Assembly election in 1993, had won 11 seats, while a breakaway PPP faction led by Bhutto's estranged sister-in-law Ghinwa Bhutto had gained one seat.
Charismatic cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan failed to win in any constituency where results had been declared.
President Farooq Leghari, once a Bhutto ally, called the polls after sacking her government on November 5, alleging corruption and misrule. Bhutto denies the charges.
Sharif, a Lahore-based industrialist who led Pakistan from 1990 to 1993, said the PML would restore stability.

"This country needs a strong and stable government and we have a very strong mandate," he said. "We thought before the elections we would have a comfortable majority, and I think we have a better than comfortable majority."

He said his first priority for the economy would be to deliver "clean, good, honest government" that would aim to cut spending, create an investment climate to attract foreign and domestic investors, and rationalise the tax system.
The past four governments, including two led by Benazir Bhutto and one by Sharif, have been sacked by presidents, who have controversial powers to dissolve the National Assembly.
A humiliated Bhutto, due to appear at a news conference at 6.30 p.m. (1330 GMT), weighed her options.
Sources in her battered PPP said she might decide after meeting party leaders in Islamabad on Wednesday to boycott the results.

PPP leaders have alleged widespread vote-rigging and irregularities in Monday's elections, but foreign election observers say they saw nothing that would have altered the outcome -- a stinging defeat for Bhutto.

Turnout was low in Monday's elections at the end of a lacklustre campaign during the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan. No official figures were available, but commentators said it was between 30 and 40 percent of the 56.5 million eligible voters.
The MQM complained of irregularities and intimidation by the splinter MQM-Haqiqi faction, but the head of a Commonwealth team of observers said the voting had been free and mainly peaceful.
"We are satisfied that all those who wished to vote were able to do so and express their own wishes at the ballot box," former Australian prime minister Sir Malcolm Fraser said.
Nevertheless, 10 people were killed in election day violence around the country, officials said.
The Karachi stock market welcomed the election result with a buying spree that sent the 100-share index soaring 52.86 points, or 3.31 percent, to close at 1,650.12 points, dealers said.
